questions.stem: At 19:30 in ED, Jane (68) opens her eyes only to voice, is confused, and does not obey commands. You now need to find out whether she localises to a painful stimulus. Which stimulus should you use?
options: Fingertip pressure on the side of a finger with a pen
Trapezius pinch or supraorbital notch pressure
A loud command close to the ear with a shoulder shake
questions.why: Localising means the hand moves to a central stimulus above the clavicle. Trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure is the standard central stimulus. Fingertip pressure is used for eye opening and for telling flexion from extension.
notes: Fingertip pressure is a peripheral stimulus. It tests eye opening and flexion, but she cannot localise to it because the hand being pressed is the one that would have to move.
Sternal rub is not a recommended standard stimulus: it is hard to apply consistently, causes bruising, and gives poorly reproducible responses.
A loud voice and a shoulder shake test eye opening to sound. They are not a painful stimulus and cannot test for localising.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, weighs 68 kg and has a creatinine of 72 µmol/L (eGFR 85). She takes weekly methotrexate and intermittent prednisolone. CSF HSV-1 PCR has just come back positive. Which antiviral regimen should she continue?
options: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for at least 21 days
Aciclovir 5 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for 7 to 10 days
questions.why: HSV encephalitis is treated with IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for at least 14 days, extended to 21 days in immunosuppressed patients. Use her actual weight, keep her hydrated, and only reduce the dose for renal impairment.
notes: 5 mg/kg is the dose for mucocutaneous HSV. It is too low for encephalitis, and 7 to 10 days is too short.
Oral valaciclovir does not reliably reach adequate CNS levels for acute encephalitis, and she is drowsy and vomiting. Treatment must be IV.
12-hourly dosing is a reduction for renal impairment, and her CrCl of about 70 mL/min does not need one. 14 days is also too short given her immunosuppression.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, has HSV encephalitis and is charted aciclovir 680 mg IV 8-hourly. The ED nurse asks why you want her kept well hydrated, with her creatinine checked daily. What is the main mechanism of aciclovir kidney injury?
options: Afferent arteriolar constriction from reduced renal prostaglandins
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis from viral antigen deposition
Efferent arteriolar dilation lowering glomerular filtration pressure
Crystal precipitation in the renal tubules when urine flow is low
questions.why: Aciclovir is excreted unchanged by the kidney and dissolves poorly in urine. High IV doses with low urine flow let it crystallise in the tubules and cause obstructive AKI. Hydration and slow infusion prevent this.
notes: Afferent constriction from prostaglandin inhibition is how NSAIDs injure the kidney, not aciclovir.
HSV does not cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, and this would not explain why hydration protects the kidney during aciclovir treatment.
Efferent arteriolar dilation is how ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR. It has nothing to do with aciclovir.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, with HSV-1 encephalitis, has a CT showing left anteromedial temporal hypodensity and pauses to find words. She also has right arm weakness (4/5) with pins and needles. Involvement of which area best explains her arm signs?
options: Left anteromedial temporal lobe and hippocampus
Left lateral precentral and postcentral gyri
Right lateral precentral and postcentral gyri
Left paracentral lobule on the medial surface
questions.why: The arm is represented on the lateral convexity of the primary motor (precentral) and sensory (postcentral) cortex. Corticospinal and sensory pathways cross, so right arm signs mean the left hemisphere is involved, beyond the medial temporal change seen on CT. MRI shows this spread better than CT.
notes: The anteromedial temporal lobe has no primary motor or sensory cortex; it explains her memory, behaviour and language problems but not her arm signs.
A right-sided cortical lesion would affect the left arm, because the motor and sensory pathways cross.
The paracentral lobule on the medial surface represents the leg and foot, which are normal in Jane.
